--- execute: freeze: auto --- # Methods ## Data retrieval ::: callout-note We downloaded data for this report on the 2026-01-02 and the raw download contained 14923 records ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Source code"} The data retrieval workflow can be found [here](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/01_ala_data_retrieval_mygalomorph.Rmd) ::: We used data from [Atlas of Living Australia (ALA)]() for this study. We downloaded occurrence records using the `galah` [R package]() using the following criteria: 1. Found in Australian mainland or Tasmania. 2. Identified to a taxon rank of species. 3. Basis of record of either: i) Preserved specimen ii) Material sample iii) Machine observation iv) Human observation 4. Coordinate uncertainty of less than 1000 meters or has a value of NA (citizen science records or human observations are typically entered as NA) We also used ALA's data quality assertions to further refine our download. We excluded occurrence records using the following criteria: 1. Coordinates are equal to 0 2. Coordinates are presumed swapped e.g. when latitude is entered as longitude 3. Latitude and longitude values are presumed negated 4. Coordinates are out of range 5. Taxon excluded by the ALA 6. Taxon considered as a questionable species See @sec-assertions to learn more about which assertions we used for this project. ## Data overview ::: callout-note The full data overview report can be found [here](https://posit.cloud/content/7700631) ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Source code"} The data overview workflow can be found [here](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/02_ala_data_overview_mygalomorph.Rmd) ::: After the initial data retrieval the data were summarised to provide an overview of the number of records, species, and families represented, as well as the broad distribution of these across Australian states. The basis of records and data quality assertions were also investigated. This provided a broad overview of data quality and facilitated review by taxonomic experts. ### Species ::: {.cell} ::: There are **530 species** in total in the original download. ``` ::: ::: `PRESERVED_SPECIMEN`: An occurrence record describing a preserved specimen.\ `HUMAN_OBSERVATION`: An occurrence record describing an observation made by one or more people.\ `MATERIAL_SAMPLE`: An occurrence record based on samples taken from other specimens or the environment.\ `MACHINE_OBSERVATION`: An occurrence record describing an observation made by a machine. ### Assertions {#sec-assertions} Various tests are run on occurrence data in the Atlas of Living Australia, resulting in assertions about the content and quality of the data. These assertions help users gauge whether data is fit for their purposes and allow for easy data filtering. Assertions are logical variables (`TRUE/FALSE`) and take the value TRUE when they apply to the associated occurrence record. Descriptions of Assertions can be found at [here](https://github.com/AtlasOfLivingAustralia/ala-dataquality/wiki.) Here, we have focused on spatial and taxonomic assertions because accurate identification of taxa and their spatial distributions is imperative to the calculation of endemism metrics and subsequent mapping. #### Spatial assertions We investigated a range of spatial assertions and deemed the following safe to bypass when refining the data download: - `COORDINATE_UNCERTAINTY_METERS_INVALID`\ We performed visual checks and flagged records did not seem to be out of species' range. They were mostly cases where `coordinateUncertaintyinMeters` was NA. We know iNaturalist records input NA for `coordinateUncertaintyinMeters`, therefore in refining the data download we will include records where `coordinateUncertaintyinMeters` is NA or less than 1000 m. We will remove flagged values for a sensitivity analysis later on. - `COORDINATE_ROUNDED`\ The original coordinates were rounded to six decimals (\~ 1 m precision) to simplify processing. The level of precision lost will not affect the endemism analysis. The following were used to refine the data download as they indicate coordinates outside of the given country (records flagged as TRUE were excluded): - `COORDINATE_OUT_OF_RANGE` - `PRESUMED_NEGATED_LONGITUDE` - `PRESUMED_NEGATED_LATITUDE` - `PRESUMED_SWAPPED_COORDINATE` - `ZERO_COORDINATE` #### Taxonomic assertions The following assertions were used to identify taxonomic discrepancies in the data and allow for review by taxonomic experts: `TAXON_MATCH_FUZZY` - is flagged when the supplied scientific name (`raw_scientificName`) does not exactly match the taxonomic backbone of the Atlas. ## Data cleaning ::: callout-note The full data cleaning report can be found [here](https://posit.cloud/content/7700644) ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Source code"} The data cleaning workflow can be found [here](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/03_ala_data_clean_mygalomorph.Rmd) ::: The following criterion were used to identify and remove records for the biodiversity analyses: - Taxonomic errors, invalid species names or synonyms - Species introduced to Australia - Marine taxa - Records with geographic errors - Any subspecies level identifications were reclassified to species level - Duplicates ### Taxonomic errors Here we clean the data for taxonomic errors, such as misspelt and outdated names. We verified that all records have species level taxonomic data. The [Australian Faunal Directory (AFD)](https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/home) is an online catalogue of taxonomic and biological information on all animal species known to occur within Australia and its territories. We used AFD data to ensure all species names in the ALA dataset are valid. We identified 1/530 species in the ALA that did not match with names in the AFD (0.1886792%). This species, *Teyl* sp. (MYG693), although not formally named, is listed as critically endangered in Western Australia, and has been retained in the analysis. ### Introduced Species Any species which are not native to Australia were removed from our dataset. To identify all introduced species in the dataset, we used species lists from the [World Spider Catalogue (WSC)](https://wsc.nmbe.ch/) and the [Global Register of Invasive and Introduced Species (GRIIS)]((http://griis.org/)). The (WSC) is a comprehensive online database of spiders from around the world, with detailed taxonomic information, distribution maps, references and images. ::: callout-important Introduced species in the WSC matched with 0 records in our data. ::: (GRIIS) is a project by the IUCN SSC Invasive Species Specialist Group to compile annotated and verified country-wise inventories of introduced and invasive species. ::: callout-important There are no arachnids in the Australian GRIIS list ::: ::: callout-note For the purpose of this project, we conclude there are no introduced spiders in our dataset. ::: ### Marine Species The World Register of Marine Species (WoRMS) was used to identify and remove marine species from the data. WoRMS provides a authoritative and comprehensive list of names of marine organisms, including currently valid and alternative names. Using the [`worrms` R package](https://docs.ropensci.org/worrms/), we supplied our list of 530 species to the `wm_records_taxamatch()` function to check whether any our taxa are classified as marine. ::: callout-note In the case of this project, we found 0 taxa that matched with marine species in the WoRMS database. ::: ### Geographic Errors Biodiversity data, especially citizen science data can have various geographic imperfections. For example, occurrence records may include data from institutions such as botanic gardens or zoos which may not be reflective of a specie's natural range. There may be data entry errors where the default location of a taxa is assumed to be the center of particular region. For these reasons, we used the R package [`CoordinateCleaner`](https://docs.ropensci.org/CoordinateCleaner/index.html) to investigate potential errors in our dataset. We used the `clean_coordinates()` function and tested whether any of our coordinates were the following: - General coordinate validity - Country and province centroids - Capital coordinates - Coordinates of biodiversity institutions - Spatial outliers - Temporal outliers - Assigned to the location of the GBIF headquarters - Located in Urban areas - Located in the sea - Duplicated values - Plain zeros Table of the number of observations flagged by CoordinateCleaner's testing suite: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Test Number of Observations
.val 0
.equ 0
.zer 0
.cap 70
.cen 0
.sea 618
.urb 2314
.otl 154
.gbf 0
.inst 27
.summary 3057
``` ::: ::: CoordinateCleaner, identified a large number of duplicates which we have a separate workflow in @sec-dups so we decided to ignore the duplicates flagged by CoordinateCleaner. After some consideration: - 70 records excluded due to being near a capital vicinity (0.47%) - 27 records excluded due to being in the vicinity of biodiversity institutions (0.18%). - 618 records excluded due to being in sea (4.14%). ::: callout-note After removing these geographic errors, we have 14205 observations after the exclusion, 512 species. ::: ### Duplicate Records {#sec-dups} Duplicate records can affect statistical analyses by pseudoreplication (increasing sample size but not adding information). We noticed that some records that had the *same* coordinate values for a large number of *different* species. These records were typically from museum record providers, we suspect this was due to the sampling method e.g. pitfall traps. For this reason, we decided to remove records if they fulfiled the following critiera: - the record was duplicated at the species level - had same exact coordinates - had same time and date of collection ::: callout-important Using this method, we excluded 2978 records from the dataset (20.9644491%). ::: ::: callout-note After deduplication, we have 11227 observations and 512 species. ::: ### Citizen science data While citizen science is an increasingly important source of data that informs research and management, it is impacted by high sampling bias and other data quality issues such as improper species identification. As such, we decided to conduct the analysis using multiple datasets: preserved specimen-only data (basis of record = `"PRESERVED_SPECIMEN"`), citizen science data (basis of record = `"HUMAN_OBSERVATION"`), and the full (cleaned) dataset. ::: callout-important There were 2332 records that were flagged with basis of record = `"HUMAN_OBSERVATION"`. This resulted in an exclusion of 15.63% of the original data) in the "preserved specimen only" dataset. ::: ## Generating species distributions ::: {.callout-tip title="Source code"} The alpha-hull workflow can be found [here](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/04_alphahulls_mygalomorph.Rmd) ::: Spatial data for invertebrates are typically sparse, often resulting in exclusion of entire species when using advanced spatial modelling methods such as species distribution models. One way to retain as many species as possible in a spatial analysis is to represent species range with alpha-hulls, a form of spatial polygon. An alpha-hull can be computed using a minimum of three data points, which allows the inclusion of data-deficient invertebrates in spatial analyses. Using the cleaned data, we applied the `EOO.computing()` function from R package [`ConR`](https://github.com/gdauby/ConR) to quantify alpha-hulls for all species that had at least 3 records (n = ). We used an alpha value of 2 and a buffer size of 0.000001 (which approximates to \~100m). The alpha-hull workflow is laid out in [this document](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/04_alphahulls_mygalomorph.Rmd). Alpha-hulls were converted into `SpatialPolgyon` objects using the [`sf`](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/sf/index.html) R package. Species with less than three records were then added as `MULTIPOINT` objects and the data exported for biodiversity analysis. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Alpha-hulls of Mygalomorph spiders from our cleaned dataset, with point-based records (species with < 3 records) included as black points](methods_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Biodiversity metrics ::: {.callout-tip title="Source code"} The biodiversity metrics workflow can be found [here](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot/blob/main/R/05_endemism_mygalomorph.Rmd) ::: The alphahull polygons and point-based records were transformed to Albers equal area projection (EPSG:9473) using the `project()` function from the `terra` package. In order to quantify patterns of species richness and endemism, these species distributuion data were converted into a community matrix, whereby each row in the matrix corresponds to a different site (spatial cell), while each column represents a different species. This was done using the `polys2comm()` function in the `phyloregion` R package. The entries in the matrix indicate whether a species is present in a particular cell, with a 1 for presence and 0 for absence. The resolution or grid size was set at 5 x 5 km. See [here](https://cran.r-project.org/web//packages/phyloregion/vignettes/phyloregion-intro.html) for further information. There are multiple metrics to assess which areas are of importance for Mygalomorph spiders, each with their own caveats. In order to get a fuller picture of biodiversity and, importantly, rare species that are limited in their range, it is helpful to use a combination of metrics. ### Species richness Species richness simply refers to the total number of species in an area. The `polys2comm()` function computes species richness for each cell. ### Endemism Endemism refers to the level of range restriction of species in an area, and numerous measures exist (refs). Weighted endemism is species richness inversely weighted by species ranges (Crisp et al. 2001),(Laffan and Crisp 2003),(Barnabas H. Daru et al. 2020). It gives higher weight to species with smaller ranges, emphasizing areas with many range-restricted species. WE highlights areas with a high concentration of rare species, which can be crucial for conservation efforts. There is a caveat that regions with high species richness can have inflated WE values simply because they have more species, not necessarily more endemics (https://www.jstor.org/stable/3554498). However, WE is a good measure for identification and research into the distribution and conservation of endemism hotspots (Shipley and McGuire 2022). WE was calculated using the `weighted_endemism()` function from the `phyloregion` R package. WE was fourth-root transformed prior to mapping to aid visualization. ## Correcting for sampling bias Sampling bias was estimated using a combination of sampling rate obtained from the `sampbias` package, and population density for the 2023-24 financial year (Australian Bureau of Statistics. (2023-24). Regional population. ABS. https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population/regional-population/2023-24.). Based on an input of species observation data, the `calculate_bias()` function from `sampbias` estimates sampling rate as a function of distance to geographic features including roads, cities, airports, and waterbodies. We included all of these features in the analysis and used a resolution of 0.05 decimal degrees. The sampling rate estimates were mapped using the `project_bias()` and `map_bias()` functions from `sampbias`. The sampling rate data were then extracted and log(+1) transformed to reduce skewness, before converting to a raster using the `rast()` function from the `terra` package. The community matrix created earlier was also converted to a raster. The sampling rate estimates from `sampbias` showed the influence of regional centres such as Alice Springs being similar to large metropolitan areas such as Sydney. This is unlikely, so the effect of population density was also incorporated. Sampling rate and population density were transformed to Albers equal area projection (EPSG:9473) using the `project()` function from `terra`. Sampling rate and population density were then aligned to the community matrix raster using the `resample()` function from `terra` with bilinear interpolation. Population density was also log(+1) transformed to reduce skewness. The influence of population density was estimated using a gaussian smoothing kernel with a sigma value of 50 km (influence becomes near zero at 3*sigma), which was implemented via the `focal()` function in `terra`. The sampling rate from `sampbias` and population density effect were then each standardised by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The two measures were then combined into a single measure of sampling bias by taking the average. Finally, this total sampling bias measure was normalised to a range between 1-10. To correct for sampling bias, for each spatial cell, the biodiversity measures (richness and endemism) were divided by this final sampling bias estimate. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Maps of sampling bias estimates](methods_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Hotspots 'Hotspots' were identified for each of the biodiversity metrics as the cells with values greater than the 95th percentile. ## Short-range species The above analyses provide a quantification of endemism across all mygalomorph spiders, however, there is the potential for the influence of high-endemism species to be masked by the influence of widely distributed species. As short-range endemics are of particular conservation concern due to their higher susceptibility to threats such as habitat loss, the analyses were repeated including only species with a range size less than or equal to 10,000 km2 (i.e. occupying < 401 cells). ## Current protection To assess the current level of protection of mygalomorph spider biodiversity, the overlap between hotspots and protected areas was calculated. Spatial polygons of protected areas in Australia were downloaded and cleaned using the `wdpar` R package. The proportion of species richness and endemism hotspots overlapping protected areas was then calculated and mapped. All maps were created using the `ggplot2` R package. ## Data and code availability All data and code to reproduce the R portion of our analyses can be found at our [Github repository](https://github.com/invertsau/inverthotspot).
